text: Naming gets a single resource identified once, at the moment you create it. Tags, Azure Policy, and Cost Management are what keep hundreds of those resources organized, compliant, and affordable once they're actually running in production, long after anyone remembers exactly why each one was deployed.

az group create --name rg-prod-eastus-web01 --location eastus with --tags Environment=Production CostCenter=1000 Owner=web-team attaches three key-value pairs the moment the group is created - the same --tags syntax works on az resource update for anything that already exists, so retrofitting tags onto resources deployed before a tagging policy existed is entirely possible.

Tags do real work beyond simple labeling. Cost Management can group your entire bill by CostCenter, so finance sees exactly what each department actually spent without anyone building a spreadsheet by hand. Environment lets you filter out every test resource before you panic about a cost spike. None of that reporting is possible if tags were never consistently applied in the first place.

Azure Policy enforces rules that tags alone can't, because tags only work if someone remembers to type them correctly. az policy assignment create with a built-in policy definition and a subscription scope assigns a rule that blocks any resource created without a CostCenter tag - the deployment simply fails at the ARM layer before the resource is ever created, not after someone notices it's missing in a report.

A policy's effect decides exactly what happens on a violation: Deny stops the deployment outright, Audit lets it through but flags the resource as non-compliant in reporting, Append adds a missing property automatically, and DeployIfNotExists remediates by deploying something extra, like a missing diagnostic setting. Pair policy with a budget - az consumption budget create tracks spending against a monthly threshold and fires a cost alert before the bill becomes an unpleasant surprise.

That's the full governance foundation for this chapter: subscriptions and management groups for structure, resource groups and ARM for deployment, regions and naming for organization, and tags, policy, and cost management for ongoing control. Chapter 2 moves into identity, starting with Microsoft Entra ID - what it actually is, underneath all the Azure AD history.
